Angiosperms. These are the flowering plants, and they are the most diverse and ecologically dominant plant group alive today. The key feature that defines angiosperms is that their seeds are enclosed in a fruit, which is the ripened ovary. This is the major distinction that separates them from gymnosperms, whose seeds develop naked and exposed.

Angiosperms evolved in the Early Cretaceous period and then rapidly diversified. Today they account for roughly ninety percent of all plant species, and they include nearly all of the staple food crops that humanity depends on. The group includes two major divisions: monocots, which have one cotyledon and include grasses, lilies, orchids, and palms; and dicots, which have two cotyledons and include broadleaves, legumes, and composites.

What makes angiosperms distinctive is their flowers. These are specialized reproductive structures with petals, sepals, stamens, and carpels, and they attract pollinators and facilitate diverse pollination strategies including insects, birds, wind, and water. Angiosperms employ a unique process called double fertilization. Two sperm nuclei fertilize two egg cells within the ovule, one producing the embryo and one producing the nutritive endosperm inside the seed.

Angiosperms dominate nearly every terrestrial and shallow-water habitat on Earth. They include all the major food crops: wheat, rice, corn, beans, and fruits of every description. Most wild flowering plants are angiosperms. Some angiosperms develop secondary growth and wood via cambium, but many are herbaceous plants that lack it entirely. This flexibility, allowing both trees and short-lived herbs, has been part of their success.

Angiosperms are derived from gymnosperm ancestors, and the fruit and the flower are their major innovations that set them apart. Like all plants, angiosperms are photosynthetic, and through photosynthesis they capture the sun's energy to drive the growth and diversity that makes flowering plants so dominant in the world today.
